info.description:
Signals ISN service API for managing Information Sharing Networks

## Key concepts
- **Information Sharing Network (ISN)**: a network set up for one purpose, such as sharing consignment data between traders and ports. Its members are accounts, each with its own access to the ISN (see _Who can see signals_), and it has the _signal types_ its members exchange.
- **Signal**: one piece of information shared through an ISN. There are three kinds (see _Content kinds_): a **json** record about something (e.g. a consignment), a **document** (e.g. a certificate PDF), and an **event** recording that something happened to another signal (e.g. a certificate was approved for a consignment). json signals and documents can be updated as more information becomes available, while events never change. Signals can be linked to each other, e.g. a consignment's documents and events are linked to the consignment (see _Correlation_).
- **Signal type**: one type of signal, identified by a slug and a version (e.g. `consignment/v1.0.0`). Each signal type has one content kind, and json and event signal types usually have a JSON schema that the content is checked against. New signal types can be added at any time without affecting existing ones.

The examples in these docs use consignments moving through ports, but the service is generic: the ISNs, signal types and schemas are defined by each network, so signals can carry any data the participants want to share.

## API documentation
- [/docs](/docs): using the API - authentication, finding ISNs, and submitting and searching signals
- [/admin-docs](/admin-docs): administering the service - ISNs and their permissions, signal types, routing, and accounts
- [/ui-docs](/ui-docs): the browser-based management interface

## Common Error Responses
All endpoints may return:
- `400` Malformed request (invalid json, missing required fields, etc.)
- `401` Unauthorized (invalid credentials)
- `403` Forbidden (insufficient permissions)
- `404` Resource not found (e.g. an ISN or signal type that doesn't exist or is not in use)
- `413` Request body exceeds size limit
- `429` Rate limit exceeded
- `500` Internal server error
- `504` Request timed out (`timeout`)

Individual endpoints document their specific business logic errors.

Standard error responses include a JSON response body containing `error_code`, `message` and `request_id` fields.

The /oauth endpoints return `error` (the RFC6749 standard error code), `error_code` and `error_description` fields instead.

## Request Limits
The endpoints are protected by:
- **Rate limiting**: Configurable requests per second (all endpoints)
- **Request size limits** (configurable - these are the defaults): 64KB for admin/auth endpoints, 5MB for json and event signal submissions, 20MB for document uploads

Check the `Signalsd-Max-Request-Size` response header for the configured size limit of the endpoint called.

The rate limit is set globally and prevents abuse of the service.
In production there will be additional protections in place such as per-IP rate limiting provided by the load balancer/reverse proxy.

## Authentication & Authorization

### OAuth
The signalsd backend service acts as an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server and supports web users and service accounts.

### Authentication Flows
- **Web users**: (Refresh Token Grant Type) Authentication via /api/auth/login -> receive JWT access token + HTTP-only refresh cookie -> use bearer tokens for API calls
- **Service accounts**: Clients implement OAuth Client Credentials flow -> receive JWT access token -> use bearer tokens for API calls

### Token Usage
All protected API endpoints require a valid JWT access token in the Authorization header:
```
Authorization: Bearer <jwt-access-token>
```

**Token Refresh (Service Accounts):**
- Client calls `POST /oauth/token` with `grant_type=client_credentials` in the form body, and the client ID/secret as form fields or HTTP Basic auth
- API validates credentials and issues new access token
- Client receives new bearer token for subsequent API calls

**Login (Web Users):**
- Client calls `/api/auth/login` with email and password and receives an access token in the response body. The refresh token is set as an HTTP-only cookie.

**Token Refresh (Web Users):**
- Client calls `POST /oauth/token` with `grant_type=refresh_token` in the form body (the HTTP-only refresh token cookie is sent automatically)
- API validates refresh token and issues new access token + rotated refresh cookie
- Client receives new bearer token for subsequent API calls

**Token Lifetimes:**
- Access tokens: 30 minutes
- Refresh tokens: 30 days (web users only). Each refresh issues a new refresh token valid for another 30 days, so users only need to log in again if they don't use the service for 30 days.

Each login or refresh revokes the user's other refresh tokens, so a user has one active session at a time.

The account's role and ISN permissions are included in the access token when it is issued. Changes to ISN permissions (and disabling an account) take effect when the account next gets an access token - up to 30 minutes later.
The exception is the admin endpoints, which check the account's current role and status on every request, so role changes and disabled accounts take effect on them straight away.

Changing or resetting a password ends all the user's sessions (their refresh tokens are revoked), so they will need to log in again.

### CSRF Protection
The refresh token used by the /oauth API endpoints is stored in an HttpOnly cookie (to prevent access by JavaScript)
and marked with SameSite=Strict (to prevent it from being sent in cross-site requests, mitigating CSRF).
The server also rejects POST, PUT and DELETE requests that the browser reports as coming from another origin, since SameSite treats sibling subdomains as the same site.

The other API endpoints are authenticated with bearer tokens, which browsers do not send automatically, so they are not open to CSRF.

## Browser Integrations
Browser-based apps on other sites can only call the public endpoints directly.

The other endpoints have no CORS policy, so web pages on other origins can't use them: the browser won't send an access token to them or let the page read the response.
Instead, call the API from your app's backend (or a small proxy) and pass the results to the browser. This is the "backend for frontend" pattern used by the signalsd UI.

Server-side clients (scripts, services etc) are not affected by CORS and can call any endpoint they have access to.

## Date/Time Handling

**URL Parameters**: The following ISO 8601 formats are accepted in URL query parameters:
- 2006-01-02T15:04:05Z (UTC)
- 2006-01-02T15:04:05+07:00 (with offset)
- 2006-01-02T15:04:05.999999999Z (nano precision)
- 2006-01-02 (date only, treated as start of day UTC: 2006-01-02T00:00:00Z)

Note: When including a timestamp with a timezone offset in a query parameter, encode the + sign as %2B (e.g. 2025-08-31T12:00:00%2B07:00). Otherwise, + may be interpreted as a space.

**Response Bodies**: All date/time fields in JSON responses use RFC3339 format (ISO 8601):
- Example: "2025-06-03T13:47:47.331787+01:00"

# Signals

## Content kinds
Each signal type has a `content_kind`, which determines how its signals are sent:
- **json**: JSON content, validated against the signal type's schema (unless the signal type was set up to skip validation). Sent with *Submit Signals* (or *Submit Signals via Router*).
- **document**: a file (PDF, JPEG, PNG or XML). Sent with *Upload a Document* and retrieved with *Download a Document*. Search results contain the document's metadata, not the file. A document can also have an `issuer_ref`, the reference its issuer gave it (e.g. an export health certificate number), which recipients can use to find it with the `issuer_ref` search filter (`issuer_ref` is currently only supported for documents).
- **event**: an immutable JSON record that a process waypoint has been reached for another signal (e.g. an export health certificate was approved for a consignment). Sent with *Submit Signals* (see Events below).

Search, withdrawal and batches work the same way for every kind, and search results include each signal's `content_kind`.

## Versions and resubmissions
A signal describes one thing, such as a consignment or a certificate. As more data emerges or corrections are made, you send the signal again and the service stores it as a new version of the same signal, so recipients see the latest version and can see its history.

You give each signal a `local_ref`, usually its ID in your own system, and send the same `local_ref` every time you send that signal. A `local_ref` is unique for your account, the ISN and the signal type version (sending the same `local_ref` to two ISNs or to two different signal types, creates two independent signals).

The service gives each signal a `signal_id` when it is first stored. Other participants use it to refer to your signal (e.g. when they want to link to it - see Correlation below).

When a `local_ref` is sent to the same ISN again:
- **If something changed**, a new version of the signal is stored (json and document signals).
- **If nothing changed** (the same content, and the same or no `correlation_id`), nothing is stored. The response contains the `signal_id`, `signal_version_id` and `version_number` of the existing latest version, with `unchanged: true`, so requests can be safely retried. JSON content is compared as JSON (key order and whitespace are ignored). Documents compare the file, its filename and its `issuer_ref`.
- **If the signal was withdrawn**, it is reactivated with a new version (json and document signals).
- **Events are never changed**: resubmitting an event with different content or a different `correlation_id`, or after it was withdrawn, fails with `resource_already_exists`. To correct an event, withdraw it and send a new event with a new `local_ref`.

## Batches
Each request also has a `batch_ref`: a label you choose to track your requests, e.g. one per scheduled run. Requests sent with the same `batch_ref` are added to the same batch, and *Get Batch Status* reports what was stored and what failed in it. The `batch_ref` doesn't affect how signals are stored.

## Correlation
A signal can be linked to another signal in the same ISN by setting its `correlation_id` to the other signal's `signal_id`.

Search results include each signal's `correlation_id` (null if the signal is not linked to another signal).

Search with `include_correlated=true` returns the signals linked to each result, whatever their type, and the `correlation_id` search filter returns the signals linked to one signal. To fetch the signal a result is linked to, search with `signal_id={correlation_id}` (see *Following signals* below).

**Correlate to the entity directly.** For example, correlate a consignment's documents and events to the consignment itself, not to each other. Correlation is one level deep: `include_correlated` only returns signals that are correlated directly to the returned signal.

**Correlating is sharing.** Correlating your signal to a signal created by another account is like emailing that account a copy, but with the extra controls that you can withdraw it or send new versions, and they see those changes. Unlike email:
- withdrawing a signal stops further access through the service
- if a new version changes the correlation_id, access moves with it: the owner of the newly correlated signal can see every version, and the previous owner can no longer access it through the service

## Routing
Some networks have one ISN per destination, e.g. one per port. Instead of choosing the ISN yourself, you can send signals to the router (*Submit Signals via Router* or *Upload a Document via Router*), which chooses the ISN for each signal:
- **A signal with a `correlation_id`** goes to the ISN of the signal it is linked to. Events always have one, and routed documents must have one, so they always go to the ISN of the signal they are about.
- **A json signal without one** is matched against its signal type's routing rules, e.g. on a port code in its content. The rules are set up by the service administrators (see [/admin-docs](/admin-docs)).

The response gives the `isn_slug` each signal was sent to. Combined with *Searching without naming the ISN*, this means your code doesn't need to know which ISNs exist: when a new port joins and your account is given access to its ISN, signals are routed to it and your searches find the responses, with no change to your code.

A `local_ref` is unique within an ISN, so a resent signal only updates the original if it is routed to the same ISN (see *Submit Signals via Router*).

## Partial success and resending
Signals in a request are validated and stored one at a time: the valid signals are stored and the ones that fail (e.g. content that doesn't match the schema, or an unknown `correlation_id`) are listed in the response with an error code. The response status tells you whether all, some or none of the signals were stored (see each endpoint for the details).

This is common when testing a new signal type, where some records in a large payload match the schema and others don't. Fix the failed signals and resend them. Signals that are resent unchanged are not stored again, so you can do this in either of these ways:
- **Resend the whole request.** Signals that were already stored are returned with `unchanged: true`, and only the fixed signals are stored. Note that any json signal in the request that has been withdrawn since it was sent is reactivated (withdrawn events are not reactivated - they fail with `resource_already_exists`).
- **Resend only the failures.** *Get Batch Status* lists the batch's unresolved failures.

When a whole *Submit Signals* request fails (an error response such as 400, 401, 403, 404, 413 or 500), or you get no response, nothing is recorded in the batch, so resend the whole request once the problem is fixed.

**Timeouts.** If the server's request timeout is reached partway through a request, the signals already processed stay stored and the rest are returned as `database_error` failures (which may not be recorded in the batch), so resend the whole request.

## Who can see signals
- Accounts with **read** access to an ISN can see every signal in it.
- Accounts with **write-only** access can see the signals they created, and the signals other accounts have correlated to their signals (one level deep).
- Signals in a **public** ISN can be searched by anyone, using *Signal Search (public ISNs)* (`/api/public/isn/...`). Downloading a document still needs an access token and access to the ISN.

An account can have different access in each ISN. Searches across several ISNs apply each ISN's rule to the signals in it.

Privacy between participants is set by the ISN's permissions. For example, in a network where all participants share their data with a government agency but not with each other, the participants are given write-only access and the agency is given read access.

## Events
Event signals record that a process waypoint has been reached - e.g. `ehc-approved` (an export health certificate was approved) or `departed-origin` - for the signal they are correlated to. Each waypoint is its own event signal type, so recipients choose which events they receive by choosing which event types to search or poll.
- **`correlation_id` is required**: correlate the event to the signal it is about (e.g. the consignment). Requests containing events without one are rejected.
- **`content` must include `occurred_at`**: the time the waypoint was reached, as an RFC 3339 timestamp with a time zone offset (e.g. `2026-09-27T14:02:00Z`).
- **`subject`**: if the event is about a specific version of a signal (e.g. version 3 of a document), name it in a `subject` field in `content`: `{"signal_id": "...", "version": 3}`. Always include the version - later versions of the document may be different.
- **Events are immutable** (see Versions and resubmissions).
- The service doesn't enforce an order: events are accepted in any order and can repeat (e.g. several inspections). To build a timeline, order a signal's correlated events by `occurred_at`.

Example: `{"local_ref": "ehc-approved-001", "correlation_id": "<consignment signal_id>", "content": {"occurred_at": "2026-09-27T14:02:00Z", "subject": {"signal_id": "<document signal_id>", "version": 3}, "certificate_no": "EHC-001"}}`

**Schemas for event types.** An event type's schema validates the event's `content`, as for json signal types, but:
- the service checks `occurred_at` whatever the schema says. The schema must still allow it: declare `occurred_at` (and `subject`, if the type has one) and list it as required, especially if the schema uses `"additionalProperties": false`
- `occurred_at` and `subject` are reserved - don't use them for anything else
- the service doesn't check `subject` yet, so a type whose events have a subject should require it in its schema, as `{"signal_id": <uuid>, "version": <integer>}`

## Searching without naming the ISN
When receiving a signal_id without details of the ISN it is in you can use the following endpoints:
```
GET /api/signal-types/{signal_type_slug}/v{sem_ver}/signals/search
GET /api/signals/search
```
These searches cover every ISN your account is a member of. Each result includes its `isn_slug`, `signal_type_slug` and `sem_ver`, so you can build further URLs (e.g. *Download a Document*) from it.

## Polling for changes
To find out about new and changed signals, poll the signal types you are interested in, or every signal type:
```
GET /api/signal-types/{signal_type_slug}/v{sem_ver}/signals/search?updated_since={cursor}&include_withdrawn=true
GET /api/signals/search?updated_since={cursor}&include_withdrawn=true
```
- `updated_since` returns the signals that changed (a new version was received, or the signal was withdrawn) since that time. Results are ordered by `signal_updated_at` across all your ISNs, so the last result's `signal_updated_at` is your cursor.
- Use `include_withdrawn=true`, so withdrawn signals are returned with `is_withdrawn: true` (otherwise they silently drop out of the results).
- **Polling is at-least-once, so overlap your polls**: set `updated_since` to 1 minute before your cursor, and skip the results you have already seen (the same `signal_id` and `signal_updated_at`). This is necessary because `signal_updated_at` is set when the service starts storing a signal, not when it finishes, so a signal that was still being stored when you last polled can appear with a `signal_updated_at` a little before your cursor. The 1 minute overlap makes sure your next poll picks it up.
- Search results are not paginated, so poll often enough to keep each result set small.

To poll a single ISN, use *Signal Search (private ISNs)* in the same way. The same rules apply, with results ordered by `signal_updated_at` within that ISN:
```
GET /api/isn/{isn_slug}/signal-types/{signal_type_slug}/v{sem_ver}/signals/search?updated_since={cursor}&include_withdrawn=true
```

## Following signals
**You received an event and need the signal it is about.** For example, an `ehc-approved` event is about a consignment, and you want the consignment with its documents and other events. The event's `correlation_id` is the consignment's `signal_id`:
```
GET /api/signals/search?signal_id={correlation_id}&include_correlated=true&include_withdrawn=true
```
The result is the consignment, with everything linked to it in. If the consignment was withdrawn, it is returned with `is_withdrawn: true`. Write-only accounts get an empty result if the consignment belongs to another account (see Who can see signals). The same search tells you what any `signal_id` is.

**You sent signals through the router and want the responses.** For example, you send consignments through the router, and the ports send back advice events linked to them. Poll the advice event type: the events from every port are returned, and each event's `correlation_id` is the `signal_id` the router returned for your consignment.
```
GET /api/signal-types/{advice_type}/v{sem_ver}/signals/search?updated_since={cursor}&include_withdrawn=true
```

**You keep a copy of the data.** For example, you store every consignment, and the documents and events linked to them. Poll every signal type, so you need one cursor rather than one for each signal type:
```
GET /api/signals/search?updated_since={cursor}&include_withdrawn=true
```
- store each result by `signal_id`, and use its `correlation_id` to attach it to the signal it is linked to
- if a new version links a signal to a different signal, it is returned with the new `correlation_id`
- a linked signal can arrive before the signal it is linked to, so keep it until that signal arrives
- signals of new signal types are returned too: skip the types you don't need

**You want to know when anything about one signal changes.** For example, you want an alert when a consignment gets a new version, or when a document or event is linked to it. Linking a signal to a consignment changes the linked signal, not the consignment, so polling the consignment type with `updated_since` doesn't show new documents or events. Instead, poll the consignment with everything linked to it, and compare the result with the previous poll:
```
GET /api/signals/search?signal_id={signal_id}&include_correlated=true&include_withdrawn=true
```
- a `signal_id` that wasn't there before: a signal was linked to the consignment
- a different `signal_updated_at`: a new version, or a withdrawal (`is_withdrawn: true`)
- a `signal_id` that is no longer there: the signal was linked to a different signal (or can no longer be seen)

Each poll returns the whole set, so there is no cursor to keep.
info.title: Signals ISN API

post.description:
The response body includes an access token which can be used to access the protected endpoints, assuming the account has the appropriate permissions.
The access_token is valid for 30 minutes.

As part of the login response, the server sets a http-only cookie on the client that will allow it to refresh the token (POST to the /oauth/token endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token in the form body).
The cookie's path is `/oauth`, so browsers only send it to the /oauth endpoints.
The refresh_token lasts 30 days unless it is revoked earlier.
- Each refresh issues a new refresh_token valid for another 30 days, so the user only has to log in again if they don't refresh for 30 days.
- Logging in revokes the user's other refresh tokens, so a user has one active session at a time.
- To revoke the refresh_token, call the /oauth/revoke endpoint.

The account's role and permissions are encoded as part of the jwt access token and this information is also provided in the response body.

put.description:
Changes the password of the signed-in user.

The caller must supply a valid access token and their current password. The new password must be at least 11 characters.

On success all the user's sessions are ended (their refresh tokens are revoked), including the current one, so they will need to log in again when their access token expires.

Users who have forgotten their password can't use this endpoint, since they have no current password to supply - an admin has to issue them a one-time reset link instead (see *Generate Password Reset Link* in the admin API docs).

post.description:
Registers a web user with an email address and a password.

The first user created is granted the "siteadmin" role and has super-user access to the site. Everyone who registers after that gets the "member" role.
New members can't access any information beyond the public data on the site until an admin grants them access to an ISN.

Site admins can grant other users the "isnadmin" role.
ISN admins can create ISNs and service accounts, and grant other accounts permission to read or write to the ISNs they own.

Self-service endpoint for service accounts to rotate their client secret.
This endpoint accepts expired (but not revoked) credentials, so a service account that
missed a rotation deadline can still self-serve recovery without admin intervention.
The old secret remains valid for 5 minutes after rotation to prevent race conditions
in distributed deployments or when network issues prevent clients receiving the new secret immediately
(if the response is lost, the old secret can be used to rotate again during those 5 minutes).

**Use Cases:**
- Regular credential rotation for security compliance
- Recovery from a missed rotation deadline (expired secret)
- Suspected credential compromise requiring immediate rotation

Client secrets expire after 1 year.

Credentials can be supplied as form fields or via HTTP Basic Auth (`Authorization: Basic base64(client_id:client_secret)`).

401.description: invalid_client — wrong client_id, revoked secret, or disabled account. Note: expired secrets are accepted on this endpoint; a 401 here means the secret has been explicitly revoked and an admin must reissue credentials.

get.description:
Returns the full status for all matching batches. Accounts see their own batches; site admins see all.
Both created_after and created_before must be provided.

Returns the status of a batch identified by batch_ref, scoped to the authenticated account.
The batch contains every request the account has sent with this batch_ref.

The response shows stored and failed signal counts broken down by ISN and signal type.
Where a signal is listed as 'rejected' this means the signal failed to load in this batch and has not been successfully resubmitted subsequently.

**Unresolved failures**

`unresolved_failures` lists the signals to correct and resend (see _Recovering from failures_ in the API introduction).
A failure is resolved when a later version of the signal is stored, in this batch or any other.
Signals the Signals Router could not route to an ISN (empty isn_slug) stay listed, even if the signal is stored later.

Resending a signal that is unchanged doesn't store a new version.
Unchanged signals are counted in the batch that first stored them, not the batch they were resent in.

Requests that are rejected as a whole (e.g. invalid JSON, authentication or permission errors) are not recorded, so they don't appear here.
If a request times out part way through, the signals stored before the timeout are reported.

Accounts can view their own batches. Site admins can supply ?account_id= to view another account's batch.
get a list of the configured ISNs (any authenticated account can use this endpoint - private ISNs are included)
Returns details about the ISN (any authenticated account can use this endpoint)

Get the signal types that have been added to the ISN.

is_in_use shows whether the registered signal type is enabled on this ISN.
Signal types that are disabled on the ISN are only returned when include_inactive=true.

This endpoint can be used by any authenticated account.

parameters.description: Include signal types that are disabled on the ISN
parameters.name: include_inactive

get.description:
Get a signal type that has been added to the ISN.

is_in_use shows whether the signal type is enabled on this ISN.

This endpoint can be used by any authenticated account.

post.description:
Submit JSON or event signals to an ISN (documents are sent to document signal types with Upload a Document)
- payloads must not mix signals of different types and are subject to the size limits defined on the site.

**Request structure**

The request body has two levels of wrapper around your data:
- **the request wrapper** applies to the whole request: the `batch_ref`, a label for tracking requests with *Get Batch Status*, and the `signals` array.
- **a signal wrapper** for each element of `signals` holds that signal's metadata: the `local_ref` that identifies the signal (send the same local_ref each time you send the signal, and corrections or new data are stored as new versions of it) and an optional `correlation_id` (the `signal_id` of a signal in the same ISN that this signal relates to - it can be another account's signal).
Your data goes in the signal's `content` field, and only `content` is validated against the signal type's schema.

See _Versions and resubmissions_ and _Batches_ in the API introduction for more information.

**Authentication**

Requires a valid access token.
The claims in the access token list the ISNs and signal_types that the account is permitted to use.

**Error handling**

Partial loads of the data are possible where the request is a valid format but individual signals fail to load
(e.g schema validation errors, incorrect correlation ids).
Failures are logged and trackable via the Batch Status endpoint.
The response provides an audit trail detailing the submission outcome.

Note the response structure is also used by the Signals Router endpoint, which can return results for multiple ISNs -
consequently the `Results` field is an array (one element for each ISN in the results).
There will only ever be a single entry when using this handler.

Errors that relate to the entire request  - e.g invalid json, authentication, permission and server errors (400, 401, 403, 404, 413, 500) -
return a simple error_code/error_message response rather than a detailed audit log.
The individual signal failures are not logged in this case, and the client must resupply the data once the problem is resolved.

**Retries**

Requests can be safely resent: signals that were already stored are returned with `unchanged: true` and are not stored again
(see _Recovering from failures_ in the API introduction).

**JSON Schema Validation**

the json contained in the `content` field is validated against the JSON schema specified for the signal type unless validation is disabled on the type definition.

Whether or not schema validation is enabled, the following issues create a 400 error and cause the entire payload to be rejected:
- invalid json format
- missing fields (batch_ref must be present; the array of signals must be in a json object called signals; and the content and local_ref must be present for each element of the signals array).
- a batch_ref that is longer than 128 characters or contains characters other than letters, numbers, hyphens and underscores
- an event without a correlation_id

**Partial success**

Each signal is validated and stored separately: valid signals are stored even if others in the request fail, and the failures are listed in `failed_signals`.
The response is 200 if every signal was stored, 207 if some were, and 422 if none were. See "Partial success and resending" in the introduction for how to resend the failures.

**Signal versions**

New versions are created when signals are resupplied using the same local_ref, e.g. because the client wants to correct a previously published signal.
If a signal has been withdrawn it will be reactivated if you resubmit it using the same local_ref.

A resubmission that doesn't change the signal - the same content, and the same or no correlation_id - creates no new version: the response contains the `signal_id`, `signal_version_id` and `version_number` of the existing latest version, with `unchanged: true` (so signals can be safely resent).
The content is compared as JSON, so differences in key order and whitespace are ignored.
Unchanged signals are not counted in the batch they were resent in - the existing version belongs to the batch that stored it.
Resubmitting a withdrawn signal always creates a new version (and reactivates it).

**Correlating signals**

Correlation IDs can be used to link signals together (a `correlation_id` is the `signal_id` of a previously submitted signal)
Signals can only be correlated within the same ISN.
If the supplied correlation_id is not found in the same ISN as the signal being submitted,
the response will contain a 422 or 207 status code and the error_code for the failed signal will be `invalid_correlation_id`.

**Events**

Signals sent to event signal types record that a process waypoint has been reached for another signal (e.g. an approved export health certificate is available for a consignment).
- events must have a `correlation_id` - correlate the event to the signal it is about (e.g. the consignment). Requests with events that don't have one are rejected (400)
- the `content` object must include an `occurred_at` field (directly in `content`, not nested in another object) containing an RFC 3339 timestamp with a time zone offset (e.g. 2026-09-27T14:02:00Z) - the time the waypoint was reached
- events are immutable: resubmitting an event with the same local_ref, content and correlation_id creates no new version and returns the existing version's `signal_id`, `signal_version_id` and `version_number` with `unchanged: true` (so events can be safely resent),
and resubmitting it with anything different, or after it was withdrawn, fails with `resource_already_exists`.
To correct an event, withdraw it and send a new event with a new local_ref.
- where an event is about a specific version of a signal (e.g. version 3 of a document), name it in a `subject` field in `content`: `{"signal_id": "...", "version": 3}`

Example event: `{"local_ref": "ehc-approved-001", "correlation_id": "<consignment signal_id>", "content": {"occurred_at": "2026-09-27T14:02:00Z", "subject": {"signal_id": "<document signal_id>", "version": 3}, "certificate_no": "EHC-001"}}`

422.description: Valid request format but all signals failed processing - returns detailed error information

get.description:
Search for signals in one private ISN (authentication required).
To search without naming the ISN, use *Signal Search (one signal type, across your ISNs)* or *Signal Search (all signal types, across your ISNs)*.

The endpoint returns the latest version of each signal (use `include_previous_versions=true` to see earlier versions).
Results are ordered by `signal_updated_at` (oldest first).

Accounts with read access can see all signals on the ISN.
Write-only accounts can only see the signals created by their own account, and the signals other accounts have correlated to them (including those returned with `include_correlated=true`).

**Search parameters**

At least one of these is required: `start_date` and `end_date`, `updated_since`, `account_id`, `signal_id`, `local_ref`, `issuer_ref` or `correlation_id`.
`start_date` and `end_date` must be used together. They filter on when the signal's latest version was received (`version_created_at`).

`updated_since` filters on when the signal last changed (`signal_updated_at`): a new version was received, or the signal was withdrawn.

**Polling for changes**

Polling is at-least-once: use `updated_since` as a cursor, start each poll 1 minute before the last `signal_updated_at` you received, and skip the results you have already seen (the same `signal_id` and `signal_updated_at`).
Use `include_withdrawn=true`, so signals withdrawn since your last poll are returned with `is_withdrawn: true` rather than left out of the results.
See *Polling for changes* in the API overview for more details.

**Documents**

For json signals and events, the signal data is returned in the `content` field.
Documents are files, so they are not included directly in the search results, instead the `content` field holds the document's metadata (`name`, `mime_type`, `size_bytes` and `sha256`), and the file is downloaded separately with *Download a Document*:
```
GET /api/isn/{isn_slug}/signal-types/{signal_type_slug}/v{sem_ver}/signals/{signal_id}/content?version={version_number}
```
The URL is built from the search result's `signal_type_slug`, `sem_ver`, `signal_id` and `version_number` (correlated documents are generally a different signal type from the one you searched).

post.description:
Upload a document (e.g. a PDF bill of lading) to a document signal type (JSON signals are sent with Submit Signals).

Documents are signals: they have a local_ref, versions, can be correlated with other signals and withdrawn.
The document details (name, mime_type, size_bytes and sha256) are returned as the signal content by the signal search endpoints.

**Request format**

The request is multipart/form-data with one document per request:
- send the form fields first (batch_ref, local_ref and any optional fields) - **the file must be the last part**
- the file part must be named `file` and must include a filename - the filename (without any directory path) is stored as the document's name
- only the batch_ref, local_ref, issuer_ref, correlation_id, sha256 and file fields are accepted (other fields are rejected with 400 malformed_body), and each form field value can be up to 1024 bytes
- documents can be up to 20MB by default (the `Signalsd-Max-Request-Size` response header gives the request limit, which allows an extra 64KB for the form fields). Larger uploads are rejected with 413 request_too_large

The request body looks like this:
```
--boundary
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="batch_ref"

daily-2026-09-26
--boundary
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="local_ref"

bol-0042
--boundary
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="BL-0042.pdf"
Content-Type: application/pdf

(the document bytes)
--boundary--
```

**Supported formats**

Only common business document formats can be uploaded: PDF, JPEG, PNG and XML. Other files are rejected with 415 unsupported_media_type.
The format is detected from the content of the file - the Content-Type of the file part is ignored.
XML documents must start with an XML declaration (<?xml ...?>).

The filename extension must match the format (.pdf, .jpg or .jpeg, .png, .xml - in any case), otherwise the upload is rejected with 400 malformed_body.

**Versions**

Uploads for a local_ref you have already used for this signal type version on the ISN are compared with its latest version (the same local_ref uploaded to another ISN is a separate document):
- the same file with the same filename creates no new version: the response contains the signal_id, signal_version_id and version_number of the existing latest version, with unchanged=true - so uploads can be safely retried
- a different file, or the same file with a different filename or issuer_ref, creates a new version (including a file that matches an older version)
- each upload sets the issuer_ref: omitting it when the document has one creates a new version without an issuer_ref
- re-uploading a withdrawn document creates a new version and reactivates it
- supplying a different correlation_id creates a new version with the new link (omitting correlation_id keeps the existing link)

Unchanged uploads are not counted in the batch they were sent in - the existing version belongs to the batch that stored it.
The same file uploaded with a different local_ref is a separate document.

Uploads rejected after the form fields have been read (e.g. unsupported format, a filename extension or sha256 mismatch, an invalid correlation_id, too large, no permission) are recorded against the batch (see the batch status endpoint).
Requests with missing or invalid form fields are not recorded.

**Retries**

An upload either stores a new version or stores nothing, so if an upload fails or times out, send it again.
If the first attempt was stored, the retry returns that version with unchanged=true, provided it uses the same file, the same filename, the same issuer_ref and the same (or no) correlation_id.
A retry sent while the original upload is still being processed can occasionally store an extra, identical version - this is harmless, but pollers will see one more update.
Uploads can take up to 2 minutes on the server (by default), so to avoid this set your client timeout above that.

**Optional fields**
- issuer_ref: the reference given to the document by the organization that issued it (e.g. the certificate number of an export health certificate).
It is returned with the document in search results, and recipients can find the document with the issuer_ref search filter.
Unlike local_ref it does not need to be unique, so a search by issuer_ref can return more than one document.
- correlation_id: the ID of a signal of any type in the same ISN that this document relates to (e.g. the consignment a bill of lading belongs to).
The upload is rejected with 422 invalid_correlation_id if the signal does not exist in the ISN.
(To send a document to the ISN of the signal it relates to without specifying the ISN, use _Upload a Document via Router_.)
- sha256: the sha256 of the document as lowercase hex, computed by the sender before uploading. If it does not match the uploaded file the upload is rejected with 400 malformed_body and no version is created.
Use it to confirm the document stored is exactly the one you sent. If it is omitted, the sha256 computed by the server is returned in the response and can be used to check the upload afterwards.

Withdraw a signal by local reference

Only the account's signal with this local reference on this ISN is withdrawn (a signal with the same local reference on another ISN is not affected).

Signals can only be withdrawn by the account that created the signal.

- ETag is the document's sha256 (in quotes) - use it to check the document is the one you expected

post.description:
Submit JSON or event signals without specifying a target ISN - the router resolves the ISN for each signal
(use _Upload a Document via Router_ to route documents).

**ISN resolution by correlation ID**

Where a _correlation ID_ is supplied, the routing rules do not apply and the signal
is routed to the ISN that received the correlated signal.

Events always have a correlation ID, so they are always routed to the ISN of the correlated signal.

**ISN resolution by pattern match**

If no correlation ID is supplied, the ISN is resolved using the routing rules defined for the _Signal Type_.
The rules are applied in the order defined in the _Routing Rules Config_ (first match is accepted).

**Resubmissions**

local_ref is unique per account/ISN, so a resubmitted signal only updates the original if it resolves to the same ISN.
If it resolves to a different ISN (e.g. because the routing field changed) it is stored as a new signal on that ISN, and the original signal is not changed - withdraw it if it is no longer needed.

**Resolution failures**

Each signal is validated against the signal type's schema before it is routed.

Signals that can't be routed are listed in `unroutable_signals` (and counted in `unroutable_count`):
- signals that fail schema validation (`malformed_body`, with the validation errors)
- signals that do not contain the routing field defined in the _Routing Rules Config_, or do not satisfy any of the routing rules (`invalid_request`)
- signals whose correlation_id is not found, or whose ISN is not in use (`invalid_correlation_id`)

Signals that resolve to an ISN where the account lacks access or write permission (`forbidden`), or where the ISN or signal type is not in use (`resource_not_found`),
are rejected and listed in the `failed_signals` of that ISN's result.

Unroutable and rejected signals don't stop the other signals in the request from being stored.
The response is 200 if every signal was stored, 207 if some were, and 422 if none were. See "Partial success and resending" in the introduction for how to resend the failures.

**Usage**

Other than the ISN resolution, this endpoint behaves the same way as the standard _Submit Signals_ endpoint
(request format, batches, error handling, schema validation, versions and correlation).
The response contains a result for each ISN the signals were routed to.

post.description:
Revokes credentials to prevent them being used to obtain new access tokens.
The request body must be `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` (RFC 6749).
Any access tokens already issued remain valid until they expire (30 minutes).

---

**Service Accounts — `client_credentials` grant (logout / credential rotation)**

Include in the request body:
- `grant_type=client_credentials`
- `client_id=<your_client_id>`
- `client_secret=<your_client_secret>`

Alternatively, credentials may be supplied via HTTP Basic Auth (`Authorization: Basic base64(client_id:client_secret)`).

Revokes **all** client secrets for the service account, which prevents any further token requests
until an admin reissues credentials via `POST /api/auth/service-accounts/reissue-credentials`.
This does not permanently disable the account — use `POST /api/admin/accounts/{account_id}/disable` for that.

---

**Web Users — `refresh_token` grant (logout)**

Include in the request body:
- `grant_type=refresh_token`

The refresh token is read automatically from the `refresh_token` HTTP-only cookie.
No additional form fields are required.

Revokes the current refresh token. The user must log in again to obtain a new one.

400.description: unsupported_grant_type · invalid_request · invalid_grant (refresh token missing, expired or revoked - error_code refresh_token_invalid)

post.description:
Issues a new access token. The request body must be `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` (RFC 6749).

Service accounts use the `client_credentials` grant, web users use the `refresh_token` grant - see below.

---

**Service Accounts — `client_credentials` grant**

Include in the request body:
- `grant_type=client_credentials`
- `client_id=<your_client_id>`
- `client_secret=<your_client_secret>`

Alternatively, credentials may be supplied via HTTP Basic Auth (`Authorization: Basic base64(client_id:client_secret)`).

Returns a new access token in the response body. Access tokens expire after 30 minutes.

---

**Web Users — `refresh_token` grant**

Include in the request body:
- `grant_type=refresh_token`

The refresh token is read automatically from the `refresh_token` HTTP-only cookie set during login.
No additional form fields are required.

Returns a new access token in the response body. The rotated refresh token is set as a new HTTP-only cookie
(the cookie's path is `/oauth`, so browsers only send it to the /oauth endpoints).
Access tokens expire after 30 minutes. Each refresh issues a new refresh token that expires 30 days later,
so the user only has to log in again if they don't refresh for 30 days. Refreshing revokes the user's other refresh tokens (one session per user).

401.description: invalid_client — wrong, expired, or revoked client secret. If your secret has expired, use POST /api/auth/service-accounts/rotate-secret to self-serve a new secret.
